A steel mill in 1905

A steel mill’s blast furnace and ore yard, Conemaugh Valley, 1905, as identified in the supplied image caption. A blast furnace is a large furnace used to make iron from iron ore; that iron can then be made into steel. Source record: U.S. Senate · Analysis approach: Library of Congress

Warmup / class simulation and debrief / about 10 minutes total

Steel Town: how businesses gain power

In the late 1800s, steel helped build railroads, bridges and cities. New production methods made it possible to produce more steel. Large mills needed expensive equipment, and businesses competed for customers. Some companies grew by buying competitors.

This short simulation explores how a starting advantage and fewer competing companies can change a market. It simplifies history so we can see the pattern.

Follow your teacher through the class simulation. Then return here and write one sentence for each question during the debrief.

Open the Steel Town simulation ↗

Next, investigate how a cartoonist portrayed business influence over government.

Background / about 2 minutes

Enough context to begin

Two goals: investigate a criticism of concentrated business power and learn how visual details communicate an argument.

  • Industrial growth expanded production. Large companies could also gain control over competitors, supplies, and markets.
  • The U.S. Senate is one of the two chambers of Congress. Senators help make federal laws.
  • A trust was an arrangement that let one group control several businesses. Imagine three delivery companies that keep different names but whose owners put their business shares in the hands of the same trustees. Those trustees direct all three. The names look separate, but the companies are under common control. The term also came to refer more broadly to large business combinations. This is a fictional modern example.
  • A monopoly exists when there is only one seller in a market. Imagine a town with just one internet provider and no alternative service: residents cannot switch to a competitor. A monopolist has or seeks that control. This is a fictional modern example.
  • Joseph Keppler drew this cartoon for Puck, a magazine that used humor and satire to comment on politics.
A cartoon makes a claim. It can praise, criticize, or persuade. Your task is to explain the artist’s claim using evidence from the image—and distinguish that claim from a proven fact.
Independent first look / about 2 minutes

What can you actually see?

Leave the numbers off at first. Inspect the whole image. Record two precise observations: objects, actions, words, size, or placement. Save explanations for later.

Observation vs. inference

“A door has a sign” describes something visible. “The artist wants to exclude someone” interprets it.

“I notice…” · “The image includes…”

“I wonder why…” · “What does…refer to?”

Teacher models one detail / about 3 minutes

From a detail to a meaning

Open detail 1. Listen as your teacher models how to support an interpretation. You will apply the same method to different details.

Click to open a larger detail view. Close it to return to the lesson.

1. Observe → 2. Interpret → 3. Explain

Observe: The figures have dollar signs and labels naming trusts and industries.

Interpret: They appear to represent business wealth and corporate interests.

Explain: The dollar signs connect them to money, while the written labels identify which business interests they represent.

Notice: the interpretation follows from visible evidence. We have not yet explained the entire cartoon.

Tools cartoonists use

Symbolism: an object or figure represents an idea or group.

Exaggeration: a feature is enlarged or distorted for emphasis.

Labels: written words identify people, groups, or ideas.

Contrast: differences invite comparison.

Irony: a gap between an expectation and what is shown or stated.

You do not need to find every technique. Explain what a particular choice does.

Partner investigation / about 7 minutes

Inspect. Interpret. Support.

Work through details 2, 3, and 4. Both partners inspect each detail. Discuss before writing your own response.

The wording Keppler’s audience knew

In the Gettysburg Address (1863), Abraham Lincoln described the democratic ideal of:

“government of the people, by the people, for the people”

Of the people: government belongs to the public.
By the people: its authority comes from the people.
For the people: it should serve the public’s interests.

This describes an ideal, not proof that everyone had equal political rights or influence.

Your comparison: What word does Keppler substitute for “people”? How does that change the meaning?

Read Lincoln’s wording · Library of Congress

Independent synthesis / about 5 minutes

What argument does the cartoon make?

Turn the numbers off and look at the complete image again. Connect the details to one overall interpretation.

“The cartoonist argues that… One detail supporting this is…”
“By showing…, the artist suggests… Another detail…”

“I would investigate…because it could show…” · “To check the claim about…, I would look for…”

Carry this method forward: What do I see? What might it mean? Why does that detail support my interpretation? What is the overall argument? What needs checking?
Apply the content / about 4 minutes

What does Keppler imply about power?

How would the cartoonist rate the power of each group? Read the background for each group, then place it on the continuum according to the power Keppler portrays in this cartoon. Use the image to infer his view, rather than rating the groups according to your own beliefs.

Read about each group

Power means the ability to influence choices, decisions, or outcomes. Economic power and legal authority can interact, but they are different.

Click each group. These are historical background notes; use the cartoon itself to explain how Keppler portrays their relationship.

Choose a group to compare its resources and ways of influencing decisions.

Return to the cartoon: Who has formal authority? Who does Keppler portray as having influence over that authority? What visual evidence shows the difference?

What this line measures: influence over Senate decisions as portrayed by Keppler. It does not measure human worth, every kind of power, or all historical situations. There is no single correct set of numbers: your evidence and reasoning matter.
Place each group according to Keppler’s portrayal in the cartoon.

How much influence over Senate decisions does the artist show each group having? Move each slider to represent the artist’s view. Base your placements on details in the cartoon.

Move each slider to record a placement. The starting midpoint is unplaced; arrow keys also work.

Transfer the skill / about 5 minutes

Access and influence: what can we infer?

Consider several explanations before making a judgment.

Meeting with government leaders can serve useful public purposes and can also raise questions about influence. Separate what you can observe from what you would need more evidence to know.

On September 29, 2026, President Trump hosted technology leaders and government officials at the White House. Discussion concerned AI development and safety. These photographs show different moments at that event.

Two kinds of sources

Keppler’s cartoon deliberately makes an argument using exaggeration and symbolism. A photograph records a selected moment; its angle, framing and caption shape what we see. Neither source tells us everything.

Access is an opportunity to influence decisions. A meeting alone does not prove that business leaders control government or that anyone acted improperly.

Explore the people and the setting

Hover, tap or keyboard-focus a number for the person’s name and company or government role. Labels describe roles at the time of the meeting. The numbers identify selected participants, not a complete guest list.

100%

Select a numbered person to read their name and role.

Readable key to the numbered people

    Look first: Describe one visible detail in a photograph. Keep that observation separate from your explanation of what it might mean.

    Optional hints: possible benefits and concerns

    Benefits to consider: sharing technical expertise, discussing jobs, addressing safety risks, or planning infrastructure such as electricity and data centers.

    Concerns to consider: rules favoring large companies, fewer opportunities for smaller competitors to be heard, or workers and communities having less access.

    These are starting points. The photographs do not establish that any of these things happened.

    Optional hints: compare without assuming

    Consider access to officials, where people appear, and who is included in the frame. Cartoon size is an artistic choice; a person’s size or seat in a photograph does not measure their actual power. Someone outside the frame may still have participated.

    Optional hints: evidence to investigate

    Consider an agenda, a full transcript, the rules or decisions made afterward, and who benefits or bears costs. Reports from workers, smaller businesses and affected communities could add perspectives missing from the photographs.

    Write one or two sentences per response. Several explanations can be reasonable; the quality of your evidence and reasoning matters.

    Company guide: familiar products and roles in AI

    AI is more than chatbots.

    Some companies make assistants such as ChatGPT. Others supply chips, rent computing systems, protect data, use AI in vehicles, or fund businesses. These are different roles in the same industry.

    Train an AI: develop its abilities using many examples. Run an AI: use it to answer a question or perform a task.

    Quick reference for businesses connected to the numbered people. The photographs do not show every company at the event. Government officials represent public offices rather than companies.
